key_insight: On a 3D expansion-compression cone at Mach 5–8, the shock/boundary-layer interaction is governed by how the boundary layer transitions through the expansion corner, shifting from large separation and locked shocks to smaller bubbles and faster, weaker flapping as Reynolds number rises.
engineering_relevance: The results show that non-canonical hypersonic corner geometries can relaminarize and dramatically alter separation physics, which matters for predicting heating, pressure loads, and control-surface design on high-speed vehicles.
method: High-frequency pressure sensors and high-framerate schlieren to capture unsteady shock motion.
Temperature-sensitive paint, shear-stress measurements, and oil-flow visualization to map separation and surface flow features.
Reynolds number variation at Mach 5 and Mach 8 to compare laminar, transitional, and turbulent approach conditions.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports multi-instrument experimental observations at Mach 5 and 8 showing shock position, separation-bubble size, and flapping frequency/amplitude changing systematically with Reynolds number.
watch_item: Because strong relaminarization at Mach 8 prevents fully turbulent interaction, the behavior may not generalize to canonical turbulent SWBLI models or directly extrapolate to other geometries.
paper_title: Hypersonic Shock-Wave/Boundary-Layer Interaction on a Three-Dimensional Expansion-Compression Geometry
